faq.title: What is the primary difference between Bluesky's AT Protocol and Mastodon's ActivityPub?
faq.description: In Mastodon (ActivityPub), your account identity is permanently tied to your hosting server's domain (e.g., @user@mastodon.social). If that server shuts down, you lose your handle and followers unless you migrated beforehand. In Bluesky (AT Protocol), your identity is an independent Decentralized Identifier (DID). You can switch your hosting server (PDS) at any time without losing a single follower or post.

faq.title: Can I host my own Bluesky server and keep my official Bluesky app account?
faq.description: Yes! You can run a self-hosted Personal Data Server (PDS) on a home Raspberry Pi or VPS. Your posts and media live on your hardware, but because your PDS federates with the global AT Protocol network, all Bluesky users can follow, reply, and interact with you seamlessly from the standard Bluesky mobile application.

faq.title: How do Bluesky custom algorithmic feeds work?
faq.description: Unlike traditional social platforms where a single opaque corporate algorithm dictates your feed, Bluesky separates content storage from feed generation. Anyone can program an open-source 'Feed Generator' microservice using lexical filters, AI embeddings, or chronological rules. Users can pin, subscribe to, and switch between hundreds of user-created algorithms.

html:
For two decades, social media platforms operated on a walled-garden monopoly model: Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram locked users into proprietary silos where identity, hosting, content distribution, and moderation algorithms were fused into a single corporate entity. If you wanted to leave Twitter, you were forced to abandon your social graph, your username, and years of public discourse.

The Authenticated Transfer Protocol (AT Protocol / atproto), developed by Bluesky, dismantles this centralized architecture. Built as an open, federated protocol for large-scale public conversation, the AT Protocol separates social networking into modular layers: Identity, Data Storage, Indexing, and Algorithmic Curation. By decoupling identity from server infrastructure, the AT Protocol delivers genuine account portability, allowing users to move between servers, run their own hosting hardware, and select their own curation algorithms without losing a single follower.

The 4 Architectural Pillars of the AT Protocol

To understand how Bluesky scales to tens of millions of users without central bottlenecks, one must analyze its four decoupled structural layers:

  1. Identity (DIDs & Handles): Users are identified by cryptographic Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), while human-readable handles (e.g., @username.bsky.social or custom domains like @alice.com) resolve to DIDs via DNS TXT records or HTTPS well-known paths.
  2. Personal Data Servers (PDS): The hosting node where a user's content actually lives. Your PDS holds your posts, profile metadata, likes, and follows inside cryptographically signed repositories. You can use Bluesky's default server or host your own private PDS on a \$5 VPS.
  3. Relays (Big Graph / Firehose Indexers): Relays crawl thousands of independent PDS instances via WebSocket event streams ("the firehose"). They aggregate, validate cryptographic signatures, and create massive unified index caches of the global network state.
  4. AppViews and Feed Generators: AppViews consume processed data from Relays to render consumer-facing mobile and web applications (threading replies, notification counts, search indexing). Feed Generators are standalone open-source microservices that filter the firehose into custom algorithmic feeds.

Decoupled Identity: did:plc vs. did:web

In traditional federated networks (like Mastodon / ActivityPub), your username is inextricably bound to your host server's domain (e.g., @bob@mastodon.art). If mastodon.art goes bankrupt, your identity is erased. The AT Protocol solves this using Decentralized Identifiers (W3C DIDs):

  • did:plc (Public Ledger of Coordinates): A lightweight, cryptographically auditable DID directory operated by the Bluesky consortium. Each did:plc document contains the user's public signing keys, rotation keys, and current PDS hosting endpoint. If your PDS server shuts down, you sign a rotation operation with your offline recovery key to repoint your DID to a new PDS, instantly migrating your identity and followers without downtime!
  • did:web: Binds your DID directly to your own personal domain name (e.g., did:web:alice.com). It requires zero central registry, deriving authority directly from your domain's TLS certificate and web server.

Repository Architecture: Merkle Search Trees (MST) and IPLD

Within a Personal Data Server, user data is organized not in opaque relational database rows, but as a content-addressed Merkle Search Tree (MST) formatted in InterPlanetary Linked Data (IPLD):

  • Every post, profile update, like, and repost is an immutable IPLD block identified by a cryptographic content identifier (CID) hash.
  • The repository root is signed by the user's private key (using the k256 ECDSA curve).
  • Because every update produces a new signed commit hash linked to previous commits, the entire history of a user's account forms an auditable, tamper-evident cryptographic log—similar to a Git repository!

Custom Algorithmic Feeds: Breaking the Opaque Feed Monopoly

On legacy social networks, engagement-maximizing algorithms reward outrage and rage-bait to boost advertising revenue. The AT Protocol democratizes curation through Custom Feed Generators:

A Feed Generator is an independent web service implementing the app.bsky.feed.getFeedSkeleton Lexicon API. When a user opens a custom feed (e.g., "Tech News Only", "Open Source Rust", or "Chronological Mutuals"):

  1. The user's mobile client requests the feed from the designated Feed Generator endpoint.
  2. The Feed Generator queries its local database (populated by monitoring the Relay firehose) and returns a list of post URIs matching its algorithmic criteria.
  3. The client passes those URIs to the AppView, which hydrates them with rich media, avatars, and reply counts.

Anyone with basic Python or Node.js programming skills can deploy a custom feed on platforms like Railway or Fly.io in under 30 minutes!

Step-by-Step: Setting Up Your Custom Domain Handle on Bluesky

Using a custom domain (e.g., @yourname.com) gives you instant verification and protects your brand from impersonation. Follow these steps:

  1. Open the Bluesky app and navigate to Settings > Account > Handle.
  2. Tap I have my own domain.
  3. Enter your apex domain (e.g., example.com) or subdomain (e.g., social.example.com).
  4. Bluesky provides a unique DNS TXT record value: 
    Host: _atproto.example.com
Type: TXT
Value: did=did:plc:ragtjsm2j2vknqknn3gujzq4
  5. Log into your DNS registrar (Cloudflare, Namecheap, GoDaddy), add the TXT record, and wait 60 seconds for DNS propagation.
  6. Return to Bluesky and tap Verify DNS Record. Your handle immediately switches to your custom domain, featuring an authoritative domain checkmark!

Merkle Search Trees (MST) and IPLD Radix Binary Encoding

The foundational computer science innovation that enables Bluesky to scale without centralized databases is the Merkle Search Tree (MST). An MST is a deterministic, balanced search tree that combines the logarithmic search efficiency of a B-tree with the cryptographic auditability of a Merkle tree:

  • Radix Sorting: Records inside an AT Protocol user repository are sorted by their Lexicon path strings (e.g., app.bsky.feed.post/3kn4f5...) and hashed using SHA-256.
  • Deterministic Tree Structure: Unlike traditional AVL or Red-Black trees whose final topology depends on the chronological order of inserts and deletes, an MST's structure is determined purely by the cryptographic hashes of its elements. Two independent servers inserting the identical set of 100,000 posts in completely different chronological order will generate the exact same cryptographic root CID hash!
  • Logarithmic Synchronization: When an AppView or Relay needs to synchronize updates from your PDS, it does not download your entire database. It compares MST root hashes and traverses only the differing branches, downloading updates in milliseconds with minimal network bandwidth.

The Relay Firehose: Real-Time Event Streaming over WebSockets

To ingest millions of daily posts across thousands of independent federated PDS instances, Bluesky Relays operate a massive real-time event pipeline known as the Firehose (com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos):

  1. Every time any user on any PDS publishes a post, likes a toot, or updates their profile, the PDS broadcasts an IPLD block commit over an outbound WebSocket stream.
  2. The Relay consumes this stream, verifies the ECDSA cryptographic signature against the user's DID document, unpacks the CAR (Content Addressable aRchive) file, and indexes the records.
  3. Developers building bots, moderation tools, or custom search engines can connect directly to the public Firehose WebSocket to consume every public action occurring across the entire global network in real time!

Self-Hosting Your Own Personal Data Server (PDS) with Docker

Deploying a self-hosted PDS gives you absolute physical sovereignty over your digital social media presence. Here is the operational architecture for deploying a PDS on Ubuntu Linux:

# Install official AT Protocol PDS installer
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bluesky-social/pds/main/installer.sh -o installer.sh
chmod +x installer.sh
sudo bash installer.sh

# Configure your domain and environment variables in /pds/pds.env:
PDS_HOSTNAME=pds.example.com
PDS_JWT_SECRET=your_secure_random_jwt_secret
PDS_ADMIN_PASSWORD=your_master_admin_password
PDS_PLC_ROTATION_KEY_K256_PRIVATE_KEY_HEX=your_hex_private_key
PDS_DATA_DIRECTORY=/pds/data
PDS_BLOBSTORE_DISK_LOCATION=/pds/blobs

# Launch Docker containers
sudo systemctl restart pds

Once your PDS is active, use the pdsadmin CLI tool to issue account invite codes and migrate your existing Bluesky handle directly to your self-hosted hardware.

Labeler Services: Decentralized Composable Moderation

Centralized networks force a single monolithic moderation standard on every global culture. Bluesky replaces this with Composable Moderation Labelers:

A Labeler is an independent organization or community that evaluates posts and accounts, applying cryptographically signed labels (e.g., spam, impersonation, nsfw, or fact-checked). Users can subscribe to any moderation labeler they trust. For example, a scientific community can subscribe to a labeler run by academic researchers to automatically filter medical misinformation, while a gaming community can subscribe to an anti-spoiler labeler. Because labels are completely decoupled from content hosting, no single authority can unilaterally censor discourse across the entire federated network.

Lexicons: The Standardized RPC and Data Modeling Schema

The AT Protocol defines all inter-service communications using Lexicons—strict JSON Schema definitions for remote procedure calls (XRPC) and repository records. From user profiles (app.bsky.actor.profile) to thread notifications (app.bsky.notification.listNotifications), Lexicons ensure that any developer in any programming language (Go, Python, TypeScript, Rust) can build fully compatible clients, relays, or AppViews without vendor approval.

Account Tombstoning and Cryptographic Revocation Guarantees

When an account owner chooses to permanently delete their account on the AT Protocol, the operation follows a strict cryptographic protocol known as Account Tombstoning:

  • The PDS signs an update to the user's DID PLC document setting the tombstone flag to true and rotating the active verification methods to empty sets.
  • The PDS broadcasts an IPLD deletion commit across the Firehose. Relays and AppViews verify the tombstone signature against the historical DID PLC state, purging indexed posts and blobs from search caches.
  • Because third-party scrapers may have saved historical firehose archives, true deletion on decentralized networks requires proactive data hygiene: deleting sensitive posts before triggering full account tombstoning.
